**Laila Jane Harré** (born 8 January 1966) is a New Zealand former politician and [trade unionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_union "Labor union"). Joining the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party") at 15, she left in 1989 to join the left-wing splinter party [NewLabour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NewLabour_Party_(New_Zealand) "NewLabour Party (New Zealand)"), later the [Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_(New_Zealand_political_party) "Alliance (New Zealand political party)"). She was elected to the [New Zealand Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Parliament "New Zealand Parliament") in [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_New_Zealand_general_election "1996 New Zealand general election") and re-elected in [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_New_Zealand_general_election "1999 New Zealand general election"). In her second term, she served as Minister for Women in the [Fifth Labour Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand "Fifth Labour Government of New Zealand"), overseeing the introduction of [paid parental leave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paid_parental_leave "Paid parental leave"). After long-time leader [Jim Anderton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Anderton "Jim Anderton") split from the Alliance in 2002, Harré replaced him as leader. With the party's fortunes in steep decline, it failed to win any seats in [that year's election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_New_Zealand_general_election "2002 New Zealand general election").

Harré then worked as a trade unionist for the next decade, including as secretary of the [National Distribution Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Distribution_Union "National Distribution Union"). She returned to politics as issues director for the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_Aotearoa_New_Zealand "Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand") in 2012, but left in 2014. She was then drafted as leader of [Kim Dotcom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Dotcom "Kim Dotcom")'s [Internet Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Party_(New_Zealand) "Internet Party (New Zealand)"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-internetleader-1) in alliance with the [Mana Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mana_Movement "Mana Movement"), but resigned after the party failed to win any seats in the [2014 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_Zealand_general_election "2014 New Zealand general election"). She rejoined the Labour Party in 2016, and has remained active as a commentator on politics and current affairs.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Harré's father was a social anthropologist, and the family spent a part of her childhood (including some years of primary school)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-Steely_leftie-2) living in Fiji while he studied urbanisation there.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-Herald2001-3) Her mother was an actress.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-Herald2001-3) After returning to New Zealand, she attended secondary school in [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland") at [Auckland Girls' Grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School "Auckland Girls' Grammar School"), before gaining [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") and [Bachelor of Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Laws "Bachelor of Laws") degrees at the [University of Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Auckland "University of Auckland"). At university she won the senior prizes for political studies and law and became an anti-nuclear activist.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-no_apprentice-4)

## Professional life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Professional life")]

After finishing her degree she spent 10 weeks on the [Nicaraguan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua")-[Honduran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras "Honduras") border with the "[Harry Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Holland "Harry Holland") Coffee Picking Brigade" before spending a year working at the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") on disarmament issues and as a representative of the [Women's International League for Peace and Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_International_League_for_Peace_and_Freedom "Women's International League for Peace and Freedom").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-no_apprentice-4) She then worked for some time as a [lawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawyer "Lawyer") specialising in industrial relations and [employment law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employment_law "Employment law"), and developing close links to the trade-union movement.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-IP_intro-5)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

### 1982–1996: Labour, NewLabour, and the Alliance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1982–1996: Labour, NewLabour, and the Alliance")]

Harré joined the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party") in 1982, representing the youth wing on the party's New Zealand Council. She worked in the [Beehive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beehive_(New_Zealand) "Beehive (New Zealand)") as an advisor to disarmament minister [Fran Wilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Wilde "Fran Wilde").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-no_apprentice-4) Throughout her seven-year membership of the party she was a critic of the policies advanced by [Roger Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Douglas "Roger Douglas"), who became [Minister of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(New_Zealand) "Minister of Finance (New Zealand)") when Labour won the [1984 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_New_Zealand_general_election "1984 New Zealand general election"). Douglas, an advocate of [free-market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-market "Free-market") economics, introduced a programme of radical reforms (often collectively labelled [Rogernomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogernomics "Rogernomics")) which alienated many of Labour's traditional supporters, including Harré.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-6)

In 1989, Harré resigned from the Labour Party. She became a founding member of the [NewLabour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NewLabour_Party_(New_Zealand) "NewLabour Party (New Zealand)"), an organisation started by dissident Labour MP [Jim Anderton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Anderton "Jim Anderton"). NewLabour later joined with several other parties to form the [Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_(New_Zealand_political_party) "Alliance (New Zealand political party)"). She stood for the Alliance nomination to contest the [Tamaki by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Tamaki_by-election "1992 Tamaki by-election") in 1992, but was unsuccessful.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-7) At the 1992 local-body elections she stood as a candidate for the newly created Auckland Regional Services Trust on the Alliance ticket. Harré was not elected, but polled the highest of unsuccessful candidates.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-8) The next year she stood as the Alliance candidate for the [Te Atatū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Atat%C5%AB_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Te Atatū (New Zealand electorate)") electorate in the [1993 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_New_Zealand_general_election "1993 New Zealand general election"), but was again unsuccessful, coming runner-up to Labour's [Chris Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Carter_(New_Zealand_politician) "Chris Carter (New Zealand politician)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-9)

### 1996–2002: Member of Parliament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1996–2002: Member of Parliament")]

[New Zealand Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Parliament "New Zealand Parliament")| Years | Term | Electorate | List | Party |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1996–1999 | [45th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45th_New_Zealand_Parliament "45th New Zealand Parliament") | List | 8 |  | [Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_(New_Zealand_political_party) "Alliance (New Zealand political party)") |
| 1999–2002 | [46th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/46th_New_Zealand_Parliament "46th New Zealand Parliament") | List | 6 |  | [Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_(New_Zealand_political_party) "Alliance (New Zealand political party)") |

In the [1996 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_New_Zealand_general_election "1996 New Zealand general election"), which took place under the new [MMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_Member_Proportional "Mixed Member Proportional") electoral system, the Alliance ranked Harré in eighth place on its party list. The Alliance gained a sufficient number of votes for Harré to enter parliament.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-Govt-bio-10)

After the [1999 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_New_Zealand_general_election "1999 New Zealand general election"), the Alliance formed a coalition government with Labour (which had by then backed away from many of the policies introduced by Douglas). Harré became [Minister for Women's Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Women_(New_Zealand) "Minister for Women (New Zealand)") and [Minister of Youth Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Youth_(New_Zealand) "Minister for Youth (New Zealand)") and Associate Minister of Labour and Commerce. She later gained additional responsibilities as [Minister of Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Statistics_(New_Zealand) "Minister of Statistics (New Zealand)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-Govt-bio-10)

She led the parliamentary campaign for the introduction of paid parental leave from Opposition and as a Minister sponsored the legislation to introduce 12 weeks paid parental leave in 2002.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-11) Other causes championed by Harré included legislation protecting the interests of building industry sub-contractors,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-12) significant minimum-wage increases and the reduction of age discrimination in the minimum wage.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-13) She re-launched the pay-equity debate as Minister of Women's Affairs,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-EPMU_speech-14) and a campaign to increase annual leave from three weeks to four weeks.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-EPMU_speech-14)

In late 2001, however, the Alliance began to show signs of internal strain.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-trench_war-15) In particular, some members of the party felt that it was losing its independent political identity and failing to differentiate itself from the Labour Party on issues such as free trade, tertiary-education funding and other core areas. The decision of Jim Anderton and a majority of Alliance MPs to back New Zealand's involvement in the US-led invasion of Afghanistan brought these tensions to a head, dividing the caucus and separating the parliamentary leadership from the majority in the non-parliamentary party organisation (led by [Matt McCarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_McCarten "Matt McCarten")). Harré, however, aligned herself with the grass-roots party view, and became its _de facto_ leader in parliament.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-17)

The collapse of the Alliance soon became inevitable,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-18) with Anderton and his supporters deciding to contest the [2002 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_New_Zealand_general_election "2002 New Zealand general election") as a new party (the [Progressives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Progressive_Party "New Zealand Progressive Party")). Harré, considered to be the foremost of the MPs who remained behind, was chosen to lead what remained of the Alliance into its election campaign, aiming to at least retain a presence in parliament.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-top_job-20) Harré herself was seen as the party's best chance of keeping a parliamentary seat, having a relatively strong chance of winning the seat of [Waitakere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitakere_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Waitakere (New Zealand electorate)").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-21) In the election itself, however, Harré placed second, being defeated by Labour's [Lynne Pillay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynne_Pillay "Lynne Pillay").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-2002_results-22)

The following year, Harré stepped down as leader of the Alliance, being replaced by Matt McCarten.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-helm-23) Harré was still active in the Alliance afterwards and was elected to the party executive at its annual conference in 2003. At the 2004 party conference she chose not to re-contest a position within the Alliance stating that from then on the most pragmatic approach for the Alliance would be to instead support the Greens and Maori Party.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-end-24) She was not aligned to any other political party from 2004 to 2011, but in 2012 accepted a role as issues director of the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_New_Zealand "Green Party of New Zealand").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-Greens-25)

### 2002–2014: Outside parliamentary politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2002–2014: Outside parliamentary politics")]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/64/Laila_Harre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laila_Harre.jpg)

Harré speaking outside parliament buildings in 2006

From 2002 to 2005, Harré led the industrial work of the New Zealand Nurses Organisation, including its successful pay-equity campaign for public-sector nurses. She served as General Secretary of the [National Distribution Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Distribution_Union "National Distribution Union") from 2005 to 2009,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-26) after which she joined the [Auckland Transition Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Transition_Agency "Auckland Transition Agency").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-27)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Laila_Harre_-_CTU_biennial_women%27s_conference_2009_%283718198290%29.jpg/250px-Laila_Harre_-_CTU_biennial_women%27s_conference_2009_%283718198290%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laila_Harre_-_CTU_biennial_women's_conference_2009_(3718198290).jpg)

Harré speaking at the New Zealand Council of Trade Union's biennial women's conference in 2009

Between 2010 and 2012 Harré worked for the [International Labour Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Labour_Organization "International Labour Organization") in Fiji. Subsequently, in 2012 she started work as the inaugural issues director of the Green Party,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-28) a position she resigned from in 2013. Harré quit the Green Party in protest to the way that the Greens had handled a rebuffed proposition by the Labour Party for conducting a joint electoral campaign.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-29)

Harré co-owns an Auckland restaurant, Ika, which pays a [living wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_wage "Living wage") to its staff.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-31)

### 2014: Internet Party leadership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2014: Internet Party leadership")]

On 29 May 2014, Harré was named as the first leader of New Zealand's [Internet Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Party_(New_Zealand) "Internet Party (New Zealand)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-internetleader-1) Vikram Kumar, chief executive of the Internet Party, initially approached her in early 2014 about becoming the party's leader, but Harré declined. Kumar encouraged her to meet with [Kim Dotcom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Dotcom "Kim Dotcom"), a meeting which led to Harré taking the project seriously, and subsequently accepting the offer. On announcing the decision, she stated that she got involved again in politics because she wanted to encourage young people to vote, and to re-connect disenfranchised people with the political system.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-32) The party allied with the [Mana Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mana_Party "Mana Party") to contest the 2014 election as the [Internet MANA Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Party_and_Mana_Movement "Internet Party and Mana Movement"). Harré had second place on the combined party's list.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-33)

Following the failure of Internet MANA to enter Parliament, Harré stood back from media view for several weeks before formally announcing she was stepping down as leader of the Internet Party, effective December 2014.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-Harre_resigns_as_leader-35)

Since the election, Harré has been occasionally writing on New Zealand left-wing blog site _The Daily Blog_, and undertook a "pilgrimage" across New Zealand called _Rethinking the System_.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-Harre_resigns_as_leader-35) In December 2016, Harré announced she had rejoined the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party") 27 years after she left to join NewLabour.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-36)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Harré lives in [Te Atatū Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Atat%C5%AB_Peninsula "Te Atatū Peninsula")[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-37) and is married to Barry Gribben. They met through the Labour Party and share an interest in an organic vineyard, a restaurant, and several properties.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-heraldrun-40) She also has two children.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-41)

Harré was diagnosed with [breast cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breast_cancer "Breast cancer"), and, because she has a family history of the disease, opted for a [double mastectomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_mastectomy "Double mastectomy") and breast reconstruction. She made a full recovery in 2012.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-threat-42)

Harré has run several marathons, including the [2013 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Boston_Marathon "2013 Boston Marathon"), where she was only a few hundred metres away from [the terrorist bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon_bombing "Boston Marathon bombing") that occurred near the finish line.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-heraldrun-40)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laila_Harr%C3%A9&search=father&fulltext=1#cite_note-44)

Laila Harré is a niece of philosopher and psychologist [Rom Harré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rom_Harr%C3%A9 "Rom Harré") and the sister of psychologist and environmentalist [Niki Harré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niki_Harr%C3%A9 "Niki Harré").

**Auckland Girls' Grammar School** (**AGGS**) is a New Zealand secondary school for girls located in [Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton,_New_Zealand "Newton, New Zealand"), Auckland. Established in 1878 as Auckland Girls' High School, it is one of the oldest secondary institutions in the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-3) The school closed its site temporarily in 1888 due to financial difficulties[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-4) and classes for girls were held at Auckland Grammar School[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-5) until the girls' school moved to new premises in Howe Street in 1909[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-6) and the name of the school changed to Auckland Girls' Grammar School.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-:1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-9) The school received the Goodman Fielder awards for School and Secondary School of the year in 2000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-10)

The main block is listed as a [Category 2 Historic Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_category_2_historic_places_in_Auckland "List of category 2 historic places in Auckland").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-11)

## Enrolment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Auckland_Girls%27_Grammar_School&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Enrolment")]

In 2018, Auckland Girls' Grammar School had 1,030 students enrolled and is 100% female. The number of international students was 22. As of July 2026, Auckland Girls' Grammar School has a roll of 1,191 students.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-NZ_school_roll_data-1)

As of 2026, the school has an [Equity Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_Index_(New_Zealand) "Equity Index (New Zealand)") of 485,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-NZ_school_equity_index_data-12) placing it amongst schools whose students have above average socioeconomic barriers to achievement (roughly equivalent to deciles 4 and 5 under the former [socio-economic decile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socioeconomic_decile "Socioeconomic decile") system).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-13)

**Auckland Girls' Grammar School** (**AGGS**) is a New Zealand secondary school for girls located in [Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton,_New_Zealand "Newton, New Zealand"), Auckland. Established in 1878 as Auckland Girls' High School, it is one of the oldest secondary institutions in the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-3) The school closed its site temporarily in 1888 due to financial difficulties[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-4) and classes for girls were held at Auckland Grammar School[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-5) until the girls' school moved to new premises in Howe Street in 1909[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-6) and the name of the school changed to Auckland Girls' Grammar School.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-:1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-9) The school received the Goodman Fielder awards for School and Secondary School of the year in 2000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-10)

The main block is listed as a [Category 2 Historic Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_category_2_historic_places_in_Auckland "List of category 2 historic places in Auckland").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-11)

## Enrolment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Auckland_Girls%27_Grammar_School&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Enrolment")]

In 2018, Auckland Girls' Grammar School had 1,030 students enrolled and is 100% female. The number of international students was 22. As of July 2026, Auckland Girls' Grammar School has a roll of 1,191 students.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-NZ_school_roll_data-1)

As of 2026, the school has an [Equity Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_Index_(New_Zealand) "Equity Index (New Zealand)") of 485,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-NZ_school_equity_index_data-12) placing it amongst schools whose students have above average socioeconomic barriers to achievement (roughly equivalent to deciles 4 and 5 under the former [socio-economic decile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socioeconomic_decile "Socioeconomic decile") system).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Girls'_Grammar_School#cite_note-13)

# Who is new deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell?

25 October 2025

Share

Save

[Add as preferred on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=bbc.com)

Kate Whannel Political reporter

![Image 1: PA Media Lucy Powell](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/70a7/live/f8ed4db0-b0eb-11f0-a072-177e9709dffa.jpg.webp)PA Media

Lucy Powell has been elected as deputy leader of the Labour Party, by 87,407 votes to 73,536.

Her political life started very early. Powell's mother went into labour with her on the day of the general election in 1974.

She even delayed going into hospital to make sure she could vote first.

"We used to say 'she was in Labour and she voted for Labour'," Lucy Powell [told the Political Thinking podcast.](https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/m002jllr/political-thinking-with-nick-robinson-series-2-lucy-powell)

At the age of nine, her father, a Labour activist, recruited her to help with the party's campaigning efforts. Her dad rewarded her with a one pound note.

Powell grew up in the Manchester suburb of Didsbury, an area which has been variously dubbed the "stockbroker" or "muesli" belt.

"It is posher now, it was not that posh then," she has said.

Of the 200 people at her sixth form, she says she was the only one to be accepted to Oxford University - not an achievement that made her happy at the time.

"I cried the day I got the offer," she says. "I didn't want to go."

In the end, she did go to Oxford to study chemistry but only lasted one year before heading to King's College London, where she said she "felt more comfortable".

"As a northern comprehensive girl arriving in Oxford in 1993, I was a duck out of water."

"Harry Potter had not been written then, but it was like Hogwarts," she told the i newspaper, adding that for a teenager who spent weekends clubbing at the Hacienda, the "stuffy environment" of Oxford's Somerville College did not suit her.

## [Why Labour's deputy leadership race could be a verdict on Starmer](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g5nxzzky2o)

## [Labour deputy debate exposes differences in approach](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxzpgjqd82o)

## [Labour deputy hopeful Powell attacks welfare 'errors'](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly6gevkn7zo)

After leaving university, she embarked on her political career, going to work for Labour MP (and Oscar-winning actress) Glenda Jackson and later Beverley Hughes, another Labour MP.

Between 1998 and 2005, she worked for Britain in Europe, a group campaigning in favour of the UK's membership of the EU.

In 2010, she ran Ed Miliband's successful bid to lead the Labour Party and continued working for him as his deputy chief of staff until 2012, when she won a by-election to represent the safe Labour seat of Manchester Central.

A year later she was promoted to the shadow cabinet and continued to serve in different frontbench roles until 2016.

She had been one of a few party centrists to stay in the shadow cabinet when Jeremy Corbyn, who came from the left of the party, unexpectedly became Labour leader.

However, in 2016 she quit in protest at his leadership and backed an ultimately unsuccessful coup attempt by Owen Smith.

She only returned to the shadow cabinet in 2020, when Sir Keir Starmer took over as leader and appointed her as shadow housing secretary.

When Labour won the 2024 election, she became Leader of the House of Commons, whose main job is managing government business in Parliament, as well as modernising Parliament and improving working conditions for MPs and staff.

In the major reshuffle that followed Angela Rayner's resignation in September, Powell was one of the few ministers to be sacked from government.

She described it as "kind of a shock but not a total surprise".

Asked if the prime minister gave her a reason for her demotion, she said "No, I did ask but he just said 'I need to make some changes'."

Reflecting on the possible reason, she said "I know I am not in the in-crowd. I don't play some of the parlour games".

"I have fed back things that in hindsight - I thought I was doing the job I was suppose to be doing - but perhaps it was feedback people didn't want to hear."

"Some of what I was feeding back - especially how difficult [legislation on welfare](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2zyvypmeeo)was going to be to land - I thought I was doing that to be helpful but maybe it was a message people didn't want to hear."

Ahead of the vote, she said that if she did win the deputy leadership, she did not want to be given a government role, adding that she did not want to be "constrained" by a cabinet job.

She said she viewed the deputy leader role as being a "bridge between the leadership and the members, a constant feedback loop" as well as a "campaigner-in-chief".

Asked about her vision for Labour, she said her Manchester Central constituency was made up of "classic Red Wall constituents - white working class, older voters" and "younger, liberal, left-leaning voters who haven't got that long-standing cultural loyalty to Labour".

The question for Labour, she said is "how we unite them together".

"I don't think tacking one way or tacking the other is how we do that."

She argued that Labour could achieve that by building a "fairer economy, an economy that works in the interests of the many, not the few".

Citing decisions to cut the winter fuel payment and welfare, she said: "Some of the mistakes we have made, some of the unforced errors have given a sense that we are not on the side of ordinary people."

# Who is new deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell?

25 October 2025

Share

Save

[Add as preferred on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=bbc.com)

Kate Whannel Political reporter

![Image 1: PA Media Lucy Powell](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/70a7/live/f8ed4db0-b0eb-11f0-a072-177e9709dffa.jpg.webp)PA Media

Lucy Powell has been elected as deputy leader of the Labour Party, by 87,407 votes to 73,536.

Her political life started very early. Powell's mother went into labour with her on the day of the general election in 1974.

She even delayed going into hospital to make sure she could vote first.

"We used to say 'she was in Labour and she voted for Labour'," Lucy Powell [told the Political Thinking podcast.](https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/m002jllr/political-thinking-with-nick-robinson-series-2-lucy-powell)

At the age of nine, her father, a Labour activist, recruited her to help with the party's campaigning efforts. Her dad rewarded her with a one pound note.

Powell grew up in the Manchester suburb of Didsbury, an area which has been variously dubbed the "stockbroker" or "muesli" belt.

"It is posher now, it was not that posh then," she has said.

Of the 200 people at her sixth form, she says she was the only one to be accepted to Oxford University - not an achievement that made her happy at the time.

"I cried the day I got the offer," she says. "I didn't want to go."

In the end, she did go to Oxford to study chemistry but only lasted one year before heading to King's College London, where she said she "felt more comfortable".

"As a northern comprehensive girl arriving in Oxford in 1993, I was a duck out of water."

"Harry Potter had not been written then, but it was like Hogwarts," she told the i newspaper, adding that for a teenager who spent weekends clubbing at the Hacienda, the "stuffy environment" of Oxford's Somerville College did not suit her.

## [Why Labour's deputy leadership race could be a verdict on Starmer](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g5nxzzky2o)

## [Labour deputy debate exposes differences in approach](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxzpgjqd82o)

## [Labour deputy hopeful Powell attacks welfare 'errors'](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly6gevkn7zo)

After leaving university, she embarked on her political career, going to work for Labour MP (and Oscar-winning actress) Glenda Jackson and later Beverley Hughes, another Labour MP.

Between 1998 and 2005, she worked for Britain in Europe, a group campaigning in favour of the UK's membership of the EU.

In 2010, she ran Ed Miliband's successful bid to lead the Labour Party and continued working for him as his deputy chief of staff until 2012, when she won a by-election to represent the safe Labour seat of Manchester Central.

A year later she was promoted to the shadow cabinet and continued to serve in different frontbench roles until 2016.

She had been one of a few party centrists to stay in the shadow cabinet when Jeremy Corbyn, who came from the left of the party, unexpectedly became Labour leader.

However, in 2016 she quit in protest at his leadership and backed an ultimately unsuccessful coup attempt by Owen Smith.

She only returned to the shadow cabinet in 2020, when Sir Keir Starmer took over as leader and appointed her as shadow housing secretary.

When Labour won the 2024 election, she became Leader of the House of Commons, whose main job is managing government business in Parliament, as well as modernising Parliament and improving working conditions for MPs and staff.

In the major reshuffle that followed Angela Rayner's resignation in September, Powell was one of the few ministers to be sacked from government.

She described it as "kind of a shock but not a total surprise".

Asked if the prime minister gave her a reason for her demotion, she said "No, I did ask but he just said 'I need to make some changes'."

Reflecting on the possible reason, she said "I know I am not in the in-crowd. I don't play some of the parlour games".

"I have fed back things that in hindsight - I thought I was doing the job I was suppose to be doing - but perhaps it was feedback people didn't want to hear."

"Some of what I was feeding back - especially how difficult [legislation on welfare](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2zyvypmeeo)was going to be to land - I thought I was doing that to be helpful but maybe it was a message people didn't want to hear."

Ahead of the vote, she said that if she did win the deputy leadership, she did not want to be given a government role, adding that she did not want to be "constrained" by a cabinet job.

She said she viewed the deputy leader role as being a "bridge between the leadership and the members, a constant feedback loop" as well as a "campaigner-in-chief".

Asked about her vision for Labour, she said her Manchester Central constituency was made up of "classic Red Wall constituents - white working class, older voters" and "younger, liberal, left-leaning voters who haven't got that long-standing cultural loyalty to Labour".

The question for Labour, she said is "how we unite them together".

"I don't think tacking one way or tacking the other is how we do that."

She argued that Labour could achieve that by building a "fairer economy, an economy that works in the interests of the many, not the few".

Citing decisions to cut the winter fuel payment and welfare, she said: "Some of the mistakes we have made, some of the unforced errors have given a sense that we are not on the side of ordinary people."

# Glenda Jackson: From Oscar winning actress to formidable politician

15 June 2023, 12:30pm

### The actress performed in TV, films and on stage before moving to serve as a Labour MP for 23 years.

After portraying characters hailed for their independence and conviction on the screen and stage, Glenda Jackson came to champion these attributes when she later turned her hand to politics.

Her acting career saw her star in Shakespearean productions, win two Oscars and portray numerous members of royalty.

She later gave it all up to serve as a Labour MP for 23 years and became a prominent critic of Tony Blair’s New Labour project.

![Image 3: Glenda Jackson death](https://image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/be2a3721929f814bc572be4d6226ce6eY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNjg2OTE2NTg4/2.72614843.jpg?w=640)

Glenda Jackson (PA)

Born in 1936 in Birkenhead, in Wirral, Jackson was the daughter of a bricklayer and left school at the age of 16 after she failed her school certificate.

While she was working at her local Boots store, she tipped her toe into acting by joining a friend at the YMCA amateur dramatics society.

She later won a scholarship to study at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (Rada).

After graduating, she began working in repertory theatres as an actress and stage manager.

![Image 4: Glenda Jackson death](https://image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/f50f00329240073553bbd866e65b387bY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNjg2OTE2NjMy/2.72614767.jpg?w=640)

# Glenda Jackson: From Oscar winning actress to formidable politician

15 June 2023, 12:30pm

### The actress performed in TV, films and on stage before moving to serve as a Labour MP for 23 years.

After portraying characters hailed for their independence and conviction on the screen and stage, Glenda Jackson came to champion these attributes when she later turned her hand to politics.

Her acting career saw her star in Shakespearean productions, win two Oscars and portray numerous members of royalty.

She later gave it all up to serve as a Labour MP for 23 years and became a prominent critic of Tony Blair’s New Labour project.

![Image 3: Glenda Jackson death](https://image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/be2a3721929f814bc572be4d6226ce6eY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNjg2OTE2NTg4/2.72614843.jpg?w=640)

Glenda Jackson (PA)

Born in 1936 in Birkenhead, in Wirral, Jackson was the daughter of a bricklayer and left school at the age of 16 after she failed her school certificate.

While she was working at her local Boots store, she tipped her toe into acting by joining a friend at the YMCA amateur dramatics society.

She later won a scholarship to study at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (Rada).

After graduating, she began working in repertory theatres as an actress and stage manager.

![Image 4: Glenda Jackson death](https://image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/f50f00329240073553bbd866e65b387bY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNjg2OTE2NjMy/2.72614767.jpg?w=640)

A year later, Jackson gained further notoriety in Peter Brook’s stage production of Marat/Sade.

She won her first best actress Oscar in 1970 for her role as Gudrun Brangwen in the romantic drama Women In Love, an adaptation of D H Lawrence’s novel of the same name.

In 1973, she picked up the prestigious prize again for the romantic comedy A Touch of Class where she starred opposite George Segal in a tale about a couple who are having an affair but find themselves falling in love.

Jackson played Queen Elizabeth I in the 1971 BBC TV series Elizabeth R, which won her two Emmy awards.

She also portrayed two other royals in the same year when she starred in biographical film Mary, Queen of Scots and played Egyptian queen Cleopatra for an episode of The Morecambe & Wise Show with comedy duo Eric Morecambe and Ernie Wise.

Jackson later swapped her dazzling acting career to move into the world of politics and in 1992 she was elected as the Labour MP for Hampstead and Highgate.

She served as a junior transport minister from 1997 to 1999 during Sir Tony Blair’s government.

![Image 5: 2010 General Election campaign May 2nd](https://image.assets.pressassociation.io/v2/image/production/ea9c55a17e9436b488a297b62c259ac4Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNjg2OTE2Njc3/2.8785978.jpg?w=640)

Prime Minister Gordon Brown listens as former actress and Labour Party MP Glenda Jackson speaks during a party meeting in a pub in Kilburn, north London (ANDREW WINNING/PA)

After more than two decades, she called time on her political career and stood down as an MP at the 2015 general election.

**Amrita Shivender Singh**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-2) (born 9 February 1958), also known as **Aziza**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-NDTV-Aziza-3), is an Indian actress who mainly works in [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi") films. Singh made her acting debut with _[Betaab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betaab "Betaab")_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-4)(1983), and established herself as a leading actress of the 1980s and early 1990s.

Singh appeared as a leading lady in commercially successful films such as _[Mard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mard\_(1985\_film) "Mard (1985 film)")_ (1985), _[Chameli Ki Shaadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chameli\_Ki\_Shaadi "Chameli Ki Shaadi")_ (1986), _[Naam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naam\_(1986\_film) "Naam (1986 film)")_ (1986), _[Khudgarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khudgarz "Khudgarz")_ (1987), _[Thikana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thikana\_(1987\_film) "Thikana (1987 film)")_ (1987), _[Waaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waaris\_(1988\_film) "Waaris (1988 film)")_ (1988), _[Toofan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toofan\_(1989\_film) "Toofan (1989 film)")_ (1989), _[Dil Aashna Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dil\_Aashna\_Hai "Dil Aashna Hai")_ (1992), _[Aaina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaina\_(1993\_film) "Aaina (1993 film)")_ (1993), and _[Rang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rang\_(1993\_film) "Rang (1993 film)")_ (1993). For _Aaina_, she won the [Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress").

In 1993, Singh took a break from acting. She returned to films with _[23rd March 1931: Shaheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd\_March\_1931:\_Shaheed "23rd March 1931: Shaheed")_ (2002), and received praise for her performance in _[Kalyug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyug\_(2005\_film) "Kalyug (2005 film)")_ (2005), _[Shootout at Lokhandwala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shootout\_at\_Lokhandwala "Shootout at Lokhandwala")_ ( 2007), _[2 States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2\_States\_(2014\_film) "2 States (2014 film)")_ (2014), _[Hindi Medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi\_Medium\_(film) "Hindi Medium (film)")_ (2017), and _[Badla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badla\_(2019\_film) "Badla (2019 film)")_ (2019).

Singh has also starred in the television soap opera _[Kkavyanjali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kkavyanjali "Kkavyanjali")_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-5) (2005–2006). She was married to actor [Saif Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saif_Ali_Khan "Saif Ali Khan") from 1991 to 2004, with whom she has two children, [Bollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bollywood "Bollywood") actors [Sara Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Ali_Khan "Sara Ali Khan") and [Ibrahim Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Ali_Khan_(actor) "Ibrahim Ali Khan (actor)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-6)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Amrita Singh was born 9 February 1958[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-w320-7) to _[Rukhsana Sultana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rukhsana\_Sultana "Rukhsana Sultana")_[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-TOI1-8) and an Indian Army Officer Shivinder Singh Virk, son of Sardar Jaspal Singh of Jandiala Guru in [Amritsar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amritsar "Amritsar") and of Sardarni Mohinder Kaur, daughter of the late Sir and Lady Sobha Singh of [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi") and Hadali. Amrita's aunt Raymon Singh is married to HH Raja Vijayendra Singh, the present Raja Sahib of Nalagarh [Princely State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_state "Princely state").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-11) She has a half-sister named Aneesa and a half-brother named Jaiveer from her dad's second marriage. Her father remarried when Amrita was 11 years old post his divorce with Rukshana Sultana.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-12) Her mother was a political associate of [Sanjay Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Gandhi "Sanjay Gandhi") during the [Indian Emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Emergency "Indian Emergency") in the 1970s, who became known for leading Sanjay Gandhi's [sterilisation campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India)#Forced_sterilisation "The Emergency (India)") in the [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") areas of [Old Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Delhi "Old Delhi").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-17) Through her paternal grandmother Mohinder Kaur, Amrita is the great-granddaughter of [Sobha Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobha_Singh_(builder) "Sobha Singh (builder)"), one of the builders of New Delhi, the grandniece of the late novelist [Khushwant Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khushwant_Singh "Khushwant Singh"), and great-grandniece of politician [Ujjal Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ujjal_Singh "Ujjal Singh"). The actress [Begum Para](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Begum_Para "Begum Para") is her great-aunt, whose husband, [Nasir Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Khan_(actor) "Nasir Khan (actor)"), is the brother of [Dilip Kumar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilip_Kumar "Dilip Kumar").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-TOI1-8) Singh was a childhood friend of [Shah Rukh Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah_Rukh_Khan "Shah Rukh Khan"). Their mothers often worked together in the Old Delhi area and Singh attended the same school as Khan's sister, Shahnaz.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-18)

Singh attended [Modern School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_School_(New_Delhi) "Modern School (New Delhi)") in New Delhi and is fluent in [Punjabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjabi_language "Punjabi language"), [Cantonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese "Cantonese") and [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_language "Swahili language").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-19)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1983–1993

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1983–1993")]

Singh made her [Hindi cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi_cinema "Hindi cinema") debut in 1983 with _[Betaab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betaab "Betaab")_, a highly successful romantic drama in which she was paired with [Sunny Deol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Deol "Sunny Deol"). This was quickly followed by a succession of hits, such as _[Sunny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny\_(1984\_film) "Sunny (1984 film)")_ (1984), _[Mard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mard\_(1985\_film) "Mard (1985 film)")_ (which was the biggest hit of 1985) and _[Saaheb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saaheb "Saaheb")_ (also 1985), _[Chameli Ki Shaadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chameli\_Ki\_Shaadi "Chameli Ki Shaadi")_ and _[Naam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naam\_(1986\_film) "Naam (1986 film)")_ (both 1986), _[Khudgarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khudgarz "Khudgarz")_ (1987), and _[Waaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waaris\_(1988\_film) "Waaris (1988 film)")_ (1988). Singh made a successful pair in several films, not only with [Sunny Deol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Deol "Sunny Deol"), [Sanjay Dutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Dutt "Sanjay Dutt"), and [Raj Babbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raj_Babbar "Raj Babbar"), but also with [Jeetendra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeetendra "Jeetendra"), [Vinod Khanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinod_Khanna "Vinod Khanna"), [Anil Kapoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anil_Kapoor "Anil Kapoor") and [Amitabh Bachchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amitabh_Bachchan "Amitabh Bachchan"), some of the leading actors of the 1980s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-20) As well as playing leading roles, she also played supporting negative roles in films such as _[Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raju\_Ban\_Gaya\_Gentleman "Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman")_ (1992), _[Suryavanshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suryavanshi\_(film) "Suryavanshi (film)")_ (1992) and _[Aaina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaina\_(1993\_film) "Aaina (1993 film)")_ (1993), winning the [Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress") for the lattermost.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-23) Her comic timings in films such as _Saaheb_ and _Chameli Ki Shaadi_ are still remembered. She decided to retire into family life and quit acting after her appearance in _[Rang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rang\_(1993\_film) "Rang (1993 film)")_ (1993).

### 2002–present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2002–present")]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7d/AmritaSingh.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AmritaSingh.jpg)

Singh in 2011

Singh returned to acting in 2002 with _[23rd March 1931: Shaheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd\_March\_1931:\_Shaheed "23rd March 1931: Shaheed")_, in which she played the mother of [Bhagat Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhagat_Singh "Bhagat Singh") (played by [Bobby Deol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Deol "Bobby Deol")). She joined the television industry with [Ekta Kapoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekta_Kapoor "Ekta Kapoor")'s family drama _[Kavyanjali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kavyanjali "Kavyanjali")_, which aired on [StarPlus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/StarPlus "StarPlus") in 2005. In the show, Singh was seen in a negative role that soon gained immense popularity.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-24) Later that year, she received critical acclaim for her performance in yet another negative role for the film _[Kalyug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyug\_(2005\_film) "Kalyug (2005 film)")_, which earned her a nomination for the [Filmfare Award for Best Performance in a Negative Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Award_for_Best_Performance_in_a_Negative_Role "Filmfare Award for Best Performance in a Negative Role"). In 2007, Singh played the role of gangster [Maya Dolas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Dolas "Maya Dolas")' mother, Ratnaprabha Dolas, in the [Sanjay Gupta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Gupta "Sanjay Gupta") film _[Shootout at Lokhandwala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shootout\_at\_Lokhandwala "Shootout at Lokhandwala")_, directed by Apoorva Lakhia. [Vivek Oberoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivek_Oberoi "Vivek Oberoi") played the role of Maya Dolas. Later on, she appeared in the [anthology film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthology_film "Anthology film")_[Dus Kahaniyaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dus\_Kahaniyaan "Dus Kahaniyaan"),_ where she appeared in the short story _Poornmasi_.

Continuing her acting journey, Singh was seen in _[Kajraare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kajraare "Kajraare")_ (2010), and also appeared in _[Aurangzeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb\_(film) "Aurangzeb (film)")_ (2012) under the [Yash Raj Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yash_Raj_Films "Yash Raj Films") banner, where she was paired with [Jackie Shroff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Shroff "Jackie Shroff") after almost two decades, after having paired together in _Aaina_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-25) In 2014, she was seen in _[2 States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2\_States\_(2014\_film) "2 States (2014 film)")_, produced by [Dharma Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharma_Productions "Dharma Productions"), portraying the role of co-actor [Arjun Kapoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_Kapoor "Arjun Kapoor")'s mother. The film was released on 18 April 2014, and was a critical and commercial success, and also earned Singh a second nomination for the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-26) In 2016, she appeared in _[Flying Jat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying\_Jat "Flying Jat")_ playing [Tiger Shroff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Shroff "Tiger Shroff")'s mother. In 2017, she appeared in the comedy-drama _[Hindi Medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi\_Medium "Hindi Medium")_ as a school principal. In 2019, she appeared in [Sujoy Ghosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sujoy_Ghosh "Sujoy Ghosh")'s psychological mystery thriller _[Badla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badla\_(2019\_film) "Badla (2019 film)")_, reuniting with [Amitabh Bachchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amitabh_Bachchan "Amitabh Bachchan") after 18 years. _Badla_ and Singh's performance received widespread critical acclaim upon release. The film proved to be a commercial success, and Singh's performance earned her a third nomination for the [Filmfare Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Awards "Filmfare Awards") for Best Supporting Actress.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-27)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

She married actor [Saif Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saif_Ali_Khan "Saif Ali Khan") in January 1991. Singh, who was raised as a [Sikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh "Sikh"), [converted to Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Converted_to_Islam "Converted to Islam") before marriage and took the name Aziza[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-NDTV-Aziza-3). The couple had an [Islamic wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikah "Nikah").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-tribune-28) 12 years younger, Khan is the son of former Indian test cricket captain [Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansoor_Ali_Khan_Pataudi "Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi"), the ninth [Nawab of Pataudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawab_of_Pataudi "Nawab of Pataudi") and actress [Sharmila Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharmila_Tagore "Sharmila Tagore") and is a member of the royal family of the erstwhile [Bhopal State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhopal_State "Bhopal State") and [Pataudi State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pataudi_State "Pataudi State"). Despite controversies, they remained married.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-29) She gave up acting after her marriage to Khan. After thirteen years of marriage, the couple divorced in 2004.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-30) Their daughter [Sara Ali Khan Pataudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Ali_Khan "Sara Ali Khan") was born on 12 August 1995, and son Ibrahim Ali Khan Pataudi on 5 March 2001.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-31)

## Artistry and legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Artistry and legacy")]

Singh is regarded as one of the most popular and leading actress of the 80s.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-32) Her debut film _Betaab_ made her an overnight sensation. [Sukanya Verma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukanya_Verma "Sukanya Verma") of _[Rediff.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rediff.com "Rediff.com")_ noted, "Amrita Singh is a heroine who breathed fire and shushed up anyone who dared disagree with her flare-ups and fury."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-33) Lakshana N Palat of _[Indian Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian\_Express "Indian Express")_ said that her career, comprised "a strong filmography" and noted, "With her narrowed eyes, and reverberating voice, Amrita created a new leading heroine. She has made a mark in every role that she has played — a 90’s vamp, a heroine, a mother, she has done it all."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-34) Ritika Nath of _[PTC Punjabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PTC\_Punjabi "PTC Punjabi")_ said, "From 1983 to 1993, Amrita Singh had the reigning ten years in the industry."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-35)

**Amrita Shivender Singh**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-2) (born 9 February 1958), also known as **Aziza**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-NDTV-Aziza-3), is an Indian actress who mainly works in [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi") films. Singh made her acting debut with _[Betaab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betaab "Betaab")_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-4)(1983), and established herself as a leading actress of the 1980s and early 1990s.

Singh appeared as a leading lady in commercially successful films such as _[Mard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mard\_(1985\_film) "Mard (1985 film)")_ (1985), _[Chameli Ki Shaadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chameli\_Ki\_Shaadi "Chameli Ki Shaadi")_ (1986), _[Naam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naam\_(1986\_film) "Naam (1986 film)")_ (1986), _[Khudgarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khudgarz "Khudgarz")_ (1987), _[Thikana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thikana\_(1987\_film) "Thikana (1987 film)")_ (1987), _[Waaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waaris\_(1988\_film) "Waaris (1988 film)")_ (1988), _[Toofan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toofan\_(1989\_film) "Toofan (1989 film)")_ (1989), _[Dil Aashna Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dil\_Aashna\_Hai "Dil Aashna Hai")_ (1992), _[Aaina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaina\_(1993\_film) "Aaina (1993 film)")_ (1993), and _[Rang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rang\_(1993\_film) "Rang (1993 film)")_ (1993). For _Aaina_, she won the [Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress").

In 1993, Singh took a break from acting. She returned to films with _[23rd March 1931: Shaheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd\_March\_1931:\_Shaheed "23rd March 1931: Shaheed")_ (2002), and received praise for her performance in _[Kalyug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyug\_(2005\_film) "Kalyug (2005 film)")_ (2005), _[Shootout at Lokhandwala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shootout\_at\_Lokhandwala "Shootout at Lokhandwala")_ ( 2007), _[2 States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2\_States\_(2014\_film) "2 States (2014 film)")_ (2014), _[Hindi Medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi\_Medium\_(film) "Hindi Medium (film)")_ (2017), and _[Badla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badla\_(2019\_film) "Badla (2019 film)")_ (2019).

Singh has also starred in the television soap opera _[Kkavyanjali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kkavyanjali "Kkavyanjali")_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-5) (2005–2006). She was married to actor [Saif Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saif_Ali_Khan "Saif Ali Khan") from 1991 to 2004, with whom she has two children, [Bollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bollywood "Bollywood") actors [Sara Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Ali_Khan "Sara Ali Khan") and [Ibrahim Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Ali_Khan_(actor) "Ibrahim Ali Khan (actor)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-6)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Amrita Singh was born 9 February 1958[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-w320-7) to _[Rukhsana Sultana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rukhsana\_Sultana "Rukhsana Sultana")_[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-TOI1-8) and an Indian Army Officer Shivinder Singh Virk, son of Sardar Jaspal Singh of Jandiala Guru in [Amritsar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amritsar "Amritsar") and of Sardarni Mohinder Kaur, daughter of the late Sir and Lady Sobha Singh of [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi") and Hadali. Amrita's aunt Raymon Singh is married to HH Raja Vijayendra Singh, the present Raja Sahib of Nalagarh [Princely State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_state "Princely state").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-11) She has a half-sister named Aneesa and a half-brother named Jaiveer from her dad's second marriage. Her father remarried when Amrita was 11 years old post his divorce with Rukshana Sultana.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-12) Her mother was a political associate of [Sanjay Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Gandhi "Sanjay Gandhi") during the [Indian Emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Emergency "Indian Emergency") in the 1970s, who became known for leading Sanjay Gandhi's [sterilisation campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India)#Forced_sterilisation "The Emergency (India)") in the [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") areas of [Old Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Delhi "Old Delhi").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-17) Through her paternal grandmother Mohinder Kaur, Amrita is the great-granddaughter of [Sobha Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobha_Singh_(builder) "Sobha Singh (builder)"), one of the builders of New Delhi, the grandniece of the late novelist [Khushwant Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khushwant_Singh "Khushwant Singh"), and great-grandniece of politician [Ujjal Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ujjal_Singh "Ujjal Singh"). The actress [Begum Para](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Begum_Para "Begum Para") is her great-aunt, whose husband, [Nasir Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Khan_(actor) "Nasir Khan (actor)"), is the brother of [Dilip Kumar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilip_Kumar "Dilip Kumar").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-TOI1-8) Singh was a childhood friend of [Shah Rukh Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah_Rukh_Khan "Shah Rukh Khan"). Their mothers often worked together in the Old Delhi area and Singh attended the same school as Khan's sister, Shahnaz.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-18)

Singh attended [Modern School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_School_(New_Delhi) "Modern School (New Delhi)") in New Delhi and is fluent in [Punjabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjabi_language "Punjabi language"), [Cantonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese "Cantonese") and [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_language "Swahili language").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-19)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1983–1993

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1983–1993")]

Singh made her [Hindi cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi_cinema "Hindi cinema") debut in 1983 with _[Betaab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betaab "Betaab")_, a highly successful romantic drama in which she was paired with [Sunny Deol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Deol "Sunny Deol"). This was quickly followed by a succession of hits, such as _[Sunny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny\_(1984\_film) "Sunny (1984 film)")_ (1984), _[Mard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mard\_(1985\_film) "Mard (1985 film)")_ (which was the biggest hit of 1985) and _[Saaheb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saaheb "Saaheb")_ (also 1985), _[Chameli Ki Shaadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chameli\_Ki\_Shaadi "Chameli Ki Shaadi")_ and _[Naam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naam\_(1986\_film) "Naam (1986 film)")_ (both 1986), _[Khudgarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khudgarz "Khudgarz")_ (1987), and _[Waaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waaris\_(1988\_film) "Waaris (1988 film)")_ (1988). Singh made a successful pair in several films, not only with [Sunny Deol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Deol "Sunny Deol"), [Sanjay Dutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Dutt "Sanjay Dutt"), and [Raj Babbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raj_Babbar "Raj Babbar"), but also with [Jeetendra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeetendra "Jeetendra"), [Vinod Khanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinod_Khanna "Vinod Khanna"), [Anil Kapoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anil_Kapoor "Anil Kapoor") and [Amitabh Bachchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amitabh_Bachchan "Amitabh Bachchan"), some of the leading actors of the 1980s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-20) As well as playing leading roles, she also played supporting negative roles in films such as _[Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raju\_Ban\_Gaya\_Gentleman "Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman")_ (1992), _[Suryavanshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suryavanshi\_(film) "Suryavanshi (film)")_ (1992) and _[Aaina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaina\_(1993\_film) "Aaina (1993 film)")_ (1993), winning the [Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress") for the lattermost.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-23) Her comic timings in films such as _Saaheb_ and _Chameli Ki Shaadi_ are still remembered. She decided to retire into family life and quit acting after her appearance in _[Rang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rang\_(1993\_film) "Rang (1993 film)")_ (1993).

### 2002–present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2002–present")]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7d/AmritaSingh.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AmritaSingh.jpg)

Singh in 2011

Singh returned to acting in 2002 with _[23rd March 1931: Shaheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd\_March\_1931:\_Shaheed "23rd March 1931: Shaheed")_, in which she played the mother of [Bhagat Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhagat_Singh "Bhagat Singh") (played by [Bobby Deol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Deol "Bobby Deol")). She joined the television industry with [Ekta Kapoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekta_Kapoor "Ekta Kapoor")'s family drama _[Kavyanjali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kavyanjali "Kavyanjali")_, which aired on [StarPlus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/StarPlus "StarPlus") in 2005. In the show, Singh was seen in a negative role that soon gained immense popularity.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-24) Later that year, she received critical acclaim for her performance in yet another negative role for the film _[Kalyug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyug\_(2005\_film) "Kalyug (2005 film)")_, which earned her a nomination for the [Filmfare Award for Best Performance in a Negative Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Award_for_Best_Performance_in_a_Negative_Role "Filmfare Award for Best Performance in a Negative Role"). In 2007, Singh played the role of gangster [Maya Dolas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_Dolas "Maya Dolas")' mother, Ratnaprabha Dolas, in the [Sanjay Gupta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Gupta "Sanjay Gupta") film _[Shootout at Lokhandwala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shootout\_at\_Lokhandwala "Shootout at Lokhandwala")_, directed by Apoorva Lakhia. [Vivek Oberoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivek_Oberoi "Vivek Oberoi") played the role of Maya Dolas. Later on, she appeared in the [anthology film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthology_film "Anthology film")_[Dus Kahaniyaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dus\_Kahaniyaan "Dus Kahaniyaan"),_ where she appeared in the short story _Poornmasi_.

Continuing her acting journey, Singh was seen in _[Kajraare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kajraare "Kajraare")_ (2010), and also appeared in _[Aurangzeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb\_(film) "Aurangzeb (film)")_ (2012) under the [Yash Raj Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yash_Raj_Films "Yash Raj Films") banner, where she was paired with [Jackie Shroff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Shroff "Jackie Shroff") after almost two decades, after having paired together in _Aaina_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-25) In 2014, she was seen in _[2 States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2\_States\_(2014\_film) "2 States (2014 film)")_, produced by [Dharma Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharma_Productions "Dharma Productions"), portraying the role of co-actor [Arjun Kapoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_Kapoor "Arjun Kapoor")'s mother. The film was released on 18 April 2014, and was a critical and commercial success, and also earned Singh a second nomination for the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-26) In 2016, she appeared in _[Flying Jat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying\_Jat "Flying Jat")_ playing [Tiger Shroff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Shroff "Tiger Shroff")'s mother. In 2017, she appeared in the comedy-drama _[Hindi Medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi\_Medium "Hindi Medium")_ as a school principal. In 2019, she appeared in [Sujoy Ghosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sujoy_Ghosh "Sujoy Ghosh")'s psychological mystery thriller _[Badla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badla\_(2019\_film) "Badla (2019 film)")_, reuniting with [Amitabh Bachchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amitabh_Bachchan "Amitabh Bachchan") after 18 years. _Badla_ and Singh's performance received widespread critical acclaim upon release. The film proved to be a commercial success, and Singh's performance earned her a third nomination for the [Filmfare Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Awards "Filmfare Awards") for Best Supporting Actress.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-27)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

She married actor [Saif Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saif_Ali_Khan "Saif Ali Khan") in January 1991. Singh, who was raised as a [Sikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh "Sikh"), [converted to Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Converted_to_Islam "Converted to Islam") before marriage and took the name Aziza[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-NDTV-Aziza-3). The couple had an [Islamic wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikah "Nikah").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-tribune-28) 12 years younger, Khan is the son of former Indian test cricket captain [Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansoor_Ali_Khan_Pataudi "Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi"), the ninth [Nawab of Pataudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawab_of_Pataudi "Nawab of Pataudi") and actress [Sharmila Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharmila_Tagore "Sharmila Tagore") and is a member of the royal family of the erstwhile [Bhopal State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhopal_State "Bhopal State") and [Pataudi State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pataudi_State "Pataudi State"). Despite controversies, they remained married.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-29) She gave up acting after her marriage to Khan. After thirteen years of marriage, the couple divorced in 2004.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-30) Their daughter [Sara Ali Khan Pataudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Ali_Khan "Sara Ali Khan") was born on 12 August 1995, and son Ibrahim Ali Khan Pataudi on 5 March 2001.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-31)

## Artistry and legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amrita_Singh&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Artistry and legacy")]

Singh is regarded as one of the most popular and leading actress of the 80s.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-32) Her debut film _Betaab_ made her an overnight sensation. [Sukanya Verma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukanya_Verma "Sukanya Verma") of _[Rediff.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rediff.com "Rediff.com")_ noted, "Amrita Singh is a heroine who breathed fire and shushed up anyone who dared disagree with her flare-ups and fury."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-33) Lakshana N Palat of _[Indian Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian\_Express "Indian Express")_ said that her career, comprised "a strong filmography" and noted, "With her narrowed eyes, and reverberating voice, Amrita created a new leading heroine. She has made a mark in every role that she has played — a 90’s vamp, a heroine, a mother, she has done it all."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-34) Ritika Nath of _[PTC Punjabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PTC\_Punjabi "PTC Punjabi")_ said, "From 1983 to 1993, Amrita Singh had the reigning ten years in the industry."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrita_Singh#cite_note-35)

# Top 20 Bollywood film actresses from 1990s

[Created by sahajitbro](https://www.imdb.com/user/p.s2et3fmm4hqygdzrjt5sqbbqly/?ref_=ls_usr_ov)Updated 3y ago
